# Knowing it's done

::: {.callout-note}
Draft brief, tier A. Bullets and references compiled from source discussions 01–08 (2026-11-16). `[LAB n]`, `[RESEARCH]`, `[PLAN]` and `[VERIFY]` mark what is still open. `vault:` paths point into the Obsidian vault.
:::

**Outcome (draft, #6):** the reader can tell real completion from faked work or tests, and fail loudly. Check: a stub PR and a test that asserts nothing are both caught.

## The pattern
- Decide what checks the work before the work is generated. Code "must answer acceptance criteria", by "mechanical checks as much as possible" (01).
- "you can't just accept that an output is correct, right, or good. you have to determine how you can TEST and MEASURE those things. these tests and measurements must be a part of the harness." (01)
- Check the actions as well as the result: "we've been bitten by symptom several times" (05, decision). A run can pass by doing the wrong thing, such as editing the tests or producing an empty patch. The book's version is cheap: code-checked rules on actions that must never happen (test files touched, a path outside the allowlist, no tool call) (05, Claude).
- Don't ask an LLM whether LLM-written code does what was asked: "the model will almost always answer yes" (01).
- An LLM that writes acceptance criteria "must be a separate session, and preferably a separate model" (01).
- "we must limit the chance for false, or empty passes to happen" (01).
- Every exit is typed. A cap with a checkpoint is "an input to a later decision", "not a failure to hide" (02).
- Stops must be resumable "with the LEAST rework possible". "the request to start a task from zero again should be something you have to explicitly ask for" (01).
- Retries: "is it 3, 5, or more? that will be up to the reader". The fixed part: "all code should assume something will break" (01). A retry carries the failure reasons forward (03, decision).
- A human-machine disagreement has no single rule: first find "did the human grade wrong, or did the machine grade wrong?" (05)

## How I set it up
- The implement harness checkpoints every few turns and replays its edits onto a clean pod (02, from the design). Caveat: it checkpoints every 5 turns and on non-success ends, so the end of a *successful* run can be missing from its record (05, Claude).
- The factory fails closed with a typed reason. GitHub's setup degrades instead ("Copilot will skip the remaining setup steps…") (08). A clean contrast, in a vendor's own words.

## How I decided, and what I gave up
- Even an enforced check can give up: the Stop hook is overridden after eight consecutive blocks (03). The reader has to decide how a run is marked when a gate's cap trips.
- "agents aren't magic, bro": volume is the difference. "the greater the volume, the greater the chance something gets through" (03).
- An agent allowed to change a PR until its checks go green (GitHub's Agent Merge) is a reward-hacking setup, unless the checks cover the actions too (08, with 05).

## What I use it for (worked example)
- **The 2026-10-13 audit: of 19 auto-merged PRs, 9 were fake and 6 partial.** Four specimens: a README edit, a tautological assert, unwired scripts, and a self-edit of the guard test. Shannon: "those details are fine to share" (05). Frame it as a gate being gamed (OWASP ASI10, reward hacking), not as learned cheating (07). This is a "machine graded wrong" case: "a test was wrong, and needed improvement" (05).

## Try it (kind)
- A stub PR and an assert-nothing test both fail the gate, loudly.
